title: 川田のスタジオで  (Kawada's Studio Test)

segments.t: Muranishi and Toshi arrive at a small Sapporo photo studio run by producer Kawada. Kawada warns Muranishi how dangerous the business can be, then suddenly challenges him to direct the set himself. Just follow the flow of the visit first.
何だよ、ここ。
お電話した村西です。
大丈夫かよ？
ちょっと待ってください。
手を出した知り合いは、今刑務所にいますよ。
余計なものはないほうがいい。
あなたならどう撮りますか？
トシ、ちょっと椅子をどかそうか。
その椅子、オレンジの椅子をね。
ちょっと眼鏡借りるわ。
いいんだよ、いいんだよ。
すばらしい、いいね！
Notice how Muranishi shifts from polite visitor to hands-on director the moment Kawada tests him. Let's hear the key lines.
何だよ、ここ。
'What is this place?' Toshi flips normal order for emphasis, blurting "nan da yo"—what on earth is it?—before tacking "koko", here, onto the end.
お電話した村西です。

'I am Muranishi, who called earlier.' In Japanese, descriptions sit right before the person they describe, so "odenwa shita Muranishi" literally says 'telephoned-earlier Muranishi'. Adding "o" onto "denwa", phone call, gives a crisp business polish.
大丈夫かよ？
'Is this place really okay?' "Daijoubu" is an indispensable everyday word covering 'okay', 'safe', and 'no problem'. Tacking "ka yo" onto the end turns a plain question into skeptical pushback.
ちょっと待ってください。
'Please wait a moment.' Softening "matte kudasai"—please wait—with "chotto", a little, gives you one of the most useful polite requests in all of Japanese.
手を出した知り合いは、今刑務所にいますよ。

'An acquaintance who dabbled in that is in prison right now.' "Te o dashita" literally means 'put a hand out', an idiom for getting involved in risky business. "Shiriai" is an acquaintance, and "keimusho ni imasu" says that person is currently in prison.
余計なものはないほうがいい。

'It is better not to have unnecessary things.' "Yokei na mono" names anything extra or unneeded. Pairing "nai" with "hou ga ii" builds the classic pattern for giving calm advice: 'it is better without it'.
あなたならどう撮りますか？

'If it were you, how would you shoot it?' Putting "nara" after "anata", you, sets up the hypothetical 'if it were up to you'. "Dou" asks 'how', and "torimasu" is the camera word for shooting photos or film.
トシ、ちょっと椅子をどかそうか。
'Toshi, let us move the chair out of the way.' "Isu" means chair, while "dokasou ka" softens "dokasu"—move something aside—into a friendly 'let us move it, shall we?'.
ちょっと眼鏡借りるわ。
'I am going to borrow these glasses for a bit.' "Megane" covers a pair of glasses with no plural needed, and "kariru" means to borrow. Notice "chotto" doing double duty again as 'just for a second'.
いいんだよ、いいんだよ。
'It is fine, let him go ahead.' Kawada repeats "ii n da yo", built around "ii", good or fine, plus explanatory "n da yo" to reassure his nervous crew.
すばらしい、いいね！

'Wonderful, that looks great!' "Subarashii" is high praise meaning wonderful or magnificent, followed by breezy "ii ne"—'nice, right?'—to keep energy up on set. Now let's listen to the whole studio scene again from beginning to end.
何だよ、ここ。
お電話した村西です。
大丈夫かよ？
ちょっと待ってください。
手を出した知り合いは、今刑務所にいますよ。
余計なものはないほうがいい。
あなたならどう撮りますか？
トシ、ちょっと椅子をどかそうか。
その椅子、オレンジの椅子をね。
ちょっと眼鏡借りるわ。
いいんだよ、いいんだよ。
すばらしい、いいね！
You just heard "chotto" soften both a polite 'please wait' and a quick 'let me borrow this', alongside "daijoubu" and "subarashii" at opposite ends of the mood scale. See you tomorrow.
また明日。
